idiom_name: #private fields with one mediating method (Proxy traps where whole-object interception is required)
implementation_notes: The classic wrapper object becomes a class whose state lives in #private fields: the engine enforces that they cannot be referenced outside the class, so the mediating method is the only route in and the exported constructor is the only way to create an instance. Where mediation must cover arbitrary property access - a facade over a plain data object or a membrane over objects exchanged with a callback - a Proxy with get/set/apply traps intercepts the object's internal methods and can check each operation, provided the raw target never leaves the mediator, because a proxy adds no protection to the target itself. In Node the runtime permission model (--permission) is the coarse-grained alternative, and its documentation is explicit that it is a seat belt against accidental access, not a boundary against malicious code, so it cannot be the only check where the threat is an attacker.
pitfalls: A Proxy does not virtualize private fields: a method that reads this.#x throws when invoked with a proxy as receiver, so proxying an object whose methods use # fields needs a different interposition point.
Callers that keep the raw target object bypass the proxy entirely; the mediator must be the only reference handed out.
Node's permission model documents itself as a seat belt rather than a security guarantee against malicious code - do not treat it as complete mediation.
Handing out a mutable object or array obtained through the mediator leaves an unmediated reference in the caller's hands; return frozen copies or guarded views.
